title: A sneeze leaves your body at highway speed
fact: Sneeze ejecta can exit at roughly 150–160 km/h, and the droplets travel far farther in a warm room than intuition suggests — ventilation dynamics, not just distance, decide who is exposed.
detail: Sneezing is a nervous-system reset: photic sneeze reflex makes about a quarter of people sneeze at bright sunlight, a wiring quirk called ACHOO syndrome.

title: Ancient Romans had working central heating
fact: Roman hypocausts circulated hot air from wood fires under raised floors and inside walls — comfortable villas and bathhouses two millennia before the thermostat. Some systems ran continuously for decades.
detail: The same principle (move heat by moving air) returned to European buildings only in the 19th century. The bath at Bath, England, still uses water plumbed by the Romans.

title: The Library of Alexandria had a food court
fact: The Mouseion at Alexandria was less a 'library with shelves' than a funded research campus: scholars dined together, studied anatomy, mapped stars, and edited texts — an ancient research institute with stipends.
detail: It declined over centuries of budget cuts and shifting politics, not one dramatic fire. Research funding, it turns out, is older than we think — and its politics too.

title: Bananas are all clones — one disease away from disaster
fact: Nearly every banana in a supermarket is the same Cavendish cultivar, propagated by cuttings. A single fungal race (Panama disease TR4) is sweeping plantations because the whole crop shares one immune system.
detail: The previous commercial banana, the Gros Michel, was wiped out commercially by the same disease in the 1950s. History is repeating; breeders are hedging with new cultivars.

title: The Eiffel Tower grows ~15 cm taller in summer
fact: Thermal expansion lengthens the iron lattice on hot days — measurable, and even visible in old photographs. The tower also leans slightly away from the sun, the sunlit side expanding more.
detail: Engineers accounted for this in 1889: the bolts and joints are designed with the movement budget built in from day one.

title: The first 'photograph' of a plant cell was drawn from cork
fact: Robert Hooke's 1665 Micrographia named the 'cell' from thin shavings of cork under a microscope — he saw the empty walls of dead cells and thought of monks' cells. Biology's founding word is architecture.
detail: Hooke estimated 1,259 million cells per cubic inch of cork. His counting logic was sound; the number was not bad for 1665.

title: Bees have been making honey for 100 million years
fact: Fossil bees in amber from the Cretaceous show wax-producing, nectar-feeding anatomy essentially unchanged today. Honey found in archaeological sites remains identifiable — and sometimes still edible.
detail: Honey's shelf life comes from the same chemistry bees evolved to protect larvae: low water, high acid, peroxide from an enzyme. The jar is a preservative that preserves itself.
